docs.title: Setting Up a Dev Container for Rust
Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker: have it downloaded on your device
  • Visual Studio Code (VS Code)
  • Git installed on your computer as well as basic git command knowledge
  • GitHub account that is set up

docs.title: Step 1: Creating Local Repository
docs.text:
Create a new project Directory

Open a terminal or the command prompt to run the commands. In this section we will be creating a directory and initializing it in the git repo. We will then create a README file for our project.

  1. Create a new directory for your project 
    mkdir rust-tutorial
cd rust-tutorial
  2. Initialize the new Git repository 
    git init
  3. Create the README file 
    echo "# Rust Tutorial" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Initial commit with README"

docs.title: Step 2: Create a Remote Repository on GitHub
docs.text:
1. Log in to your GitHub account and navigate to the "Create a New Repository" page.
  2. Ensure you fill in the following details:
    • Repository Name: rust-tutorial
    • Description: "Simple Rust tutorial that outputs Hello COMP423!"
    • Visibility: Public

      Note: Do not initialize the repository with a README, .gitignore, or license. You already did that using the terminal in the previous step.

  3. Click Create Repository.

docs.title: Step 3: Link the local repository to the GitHub (remote repository)
docs.text:
1. Add the GitHub repository as a remote 
    git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/rust-tutorial.git

Caution

Make sure to replace <your-username> with your GitHub username.

  1. Check what your repository's default branch is using git branch. You should expect it to indicate that your default branch is main.

Note

If your default branch is not main, rename it to main: 

git branch -M main

  1. Push your local commits to the GitHub repository. 
    git push --set-upstream origin main

Note

All the changes you have made so far should now be pushed up to remote repository and you can see this commit on GitHub as well.

docs.title: Step 1: Add Development Container Configuration
docs.text:
1. Open the rust-tutorial directory on VS Code.
    • File->Open Folder->rust-tutorial
  2. Install the Dev Containers extension for VS Code.
  3. Create a .devcontainer directory in the root of your project. Add the devcontainer.json file to the created directory. The configuration of the file should be: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json
  4. In this file, add the following code 
    {
  "name": "Rust Tutorial",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/rust:latest",
  "customizations": {
    "vscode": {
      "settings": {},
      "extensions": ["rust-lang.rust-analyzer"]
    }
  }
}

Note

name is the name of the dev container

image is the Docker image to use and in this case its the latest version of a Go envrionment

customizations adds useful configurations to VS Code,

We are adding the rust-analyzer extension via VS Code automatically whenever the container is created. It provides us with a variety of different features such as code completion, error detection, etc.

docs.title: Step 2: Reopen the project in VS Code Dev Container
docs.text: Open the project in the container by pressing Ctrl+Shift+P and typing in "Dev Containers: Reopen in Container"

docs.title: Step 3: Verify version of Rust
docs.text:
1. Verify the Rust installation by running the following code in the terminal. Open a new terminal. 
    rustc --version
    Make sure the recent version is being run to ensure the setup was successful.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Rust Project
docs.text:
1. In the project root, run the following code. 
    cargo new hello_comp423 --vcs none
cd hello_comp423

    Note: ---vcs none will create a new Rust Binary Project without making/initializing a git repository

docs.title: Step 2: Writing and running the program
docs.text:
1. Modify the main.rs file Navigate to the hello_comp423/src/main.rs file and update its contents: 
    fn main() {
    println!("Hello COMP423");
}
  2. Change into the hello_comp423 directory. 
    cd hello_comp423
  3. Compile the program 
    cargo build

Note

This will create the executable file but will not run the file till we execute the next command. This is similar to the gcc command because it will produce an executable file. We must then run this executable file to get the output for the file.

  1. Run the executable using: 
    ./target/debug/hello_comp423

docs.title: Alternative way: avoiding Build
docs.text:
1. Run the program 
    cargo run

Note

This command will compile (if needed) and run the program with one command to make the process faster. If cargo build is used, we have already completed the compile step, so this comman will just run the program files.

docs.title: Publish your Project on GitHub
docs.text:
When you are done with writing code on your project and are ready: 

git add .
git commit -m "Initial Rust dev container setup"
Push this code upto github when the remote is ready: 
git remote add origin <repo-url>
git push -u origin main

docs.title: You are all done!
docs.text: You are successfully created your first rust program. If you are followed this tutorial you have set up a proper Rust program using Dev Container on VS Code. This program should successfully output "Hello COMP423". The tutorial models professional workflows in Rust Development and dives into the basics of working with and building projets using Rust.
